prize_parts.citation: For visionary, densely patterned Romanian prose, above all Blinding and Solenoid, in which memory, the body and dream are built into a metaphysical architecture of rare imaginative scale.

statement.case_for: My laureate is unchanged: Cărtărescu (B031). The reasons are literary and do not depend on the fact that all six round-1 files point the same way. On the common criteria, the public record shows an unmistakable voice. It also shows formal ambition at very large scale, since the Orbitor project (Blinding) and Solenoid are built as long, ordered structures. And it shows an inner life treated as a world, which gives the oeuvre imaginative and intellectual depth. On the chair's first question, public descriptions of Solenoid present it in a different mode from the trilogy, a first-person, diary-like narrative anchored in an ordinary teacher's life, in which the visionary enters through the mundane. If that is right, the later book changes the architecture and not only the motifs. I hold this as a judgment from public knowledge and translation, not as a finding from close reading, and I would accept a reasoned close reading showing otherwise as evidence. On the standard of sustained quality, I keep my round-1 view. A whole-oeuvre prize recognizes the peaks and the overall direction, and it does not require every volume to be equally achieved. I would now add a limit, so that the standard is not an excuse. If the peaks are only the earlier books and the later work merely restates them, the case should be treated as weaker. On citation scope, I have changed my wording in response to colleagues. I now rest the citation on the prose and name the two works, and I leave poetry out of the text. That matches the corpus we can actually assess and avoids claiming more than translation coverage supports. The case needs no appeal to national, regional or symbolic significance, and it does not need the 'idealist' direction of Nobel's will as a separate argument.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains the one all members share. I judge long Romanian sentences, their rhythm and register, through translation and public knowledge, and these are the qualities on which the case partly rests. My answer to the repetition question is provisional, and it could be wrong. Recurrence of imagery is hard to distinguish from stalled development without close reading of specific passages, and nobody on this record has done that. There is also a risk that the standard I favor, peaks and direction, is too generous to a digressive late phase. I would be uneasy if it were applied only to the candidate who happens to lead. Finally, agreement among six members who share the same translations and the same reservations is weak evidence, because our judgments may be correlated. If close reading or external expert reports showed the late fictions circling the same material, I would move to Zurita (B005), whose project is more concentrated and whose development across volumes can be tested on the written text, or to Adonis (B020).

responses.point: Mattson ranks Cărtărescu first but asks whether the scale and recurrence of the imagery is repetition rather than development. She keeps Michon second for concentrated, singular French prose, and she says Michon's intensity, not volume, is the point.
responses.response: I take her repetition question to be the right test, and I try here to give it a more concrete form. The question is not whether motifs recur, since in a metaphysical project they will. It is whether the later book reorganizes them. My reading of the public record is that Solenoid changes the narrative mode and framing, which counts toward development, but I cannot confirm it from close reading and say so. On Michon, I do not doubt the sentence-level achievement. My difficulty is that a whole-oeuvre judgment of a very small corpus whose force sits in French syntax gives us less to test. The chair asked whether anyone wants to argue explicitly that a few books suffice. I have not seen that argument made, and I would listen to it, but on this record I do not move Michon into my configuration.

responses.point: Olsson says recurrence of imagery in a metaphysical project is partly the method. He says what matters is whether Solenoid changes the architecture, and he keeps Adonis and Tawada as alternatives for their formal invention in language.
responses.response: I agree that recurrence can be method, and I would not count it against a writer on its face. I would add that this can become an argument no evidence could refute, so we should say in advance what would count against it: later volumes that restate earlier set pieces without changing structure, perspective or stakes. On his alternatives, I ranked Adonis third and keep him as a second alternative. Fragmentation and renewal of an inherited poetic language are real formal achievements, and I have the same limit he names, that prosody and allusion are poorly carried by translation. I also noted his disclosure of scholarly overlap with the fragment and with linguistic displacement. I treat it as context, as he does, and it does not change how I read his argument for Cărtărescu.

responses.point: Palm drafts a citation that names prose and specific works and leaves poetry out. She says the case is clearest around the fiction. She also says Tawada's case depends on a two-language corpus that no single reader on the committee can judge equally.
responses.response: I now follow her scoping, and it is the main change in my configuration. My round-1 citation named prose and poetry, but the poetry is the thinnest part of what we can assess, and a citation should not claim more than the evidence supports. Naming Blinding and Solenoid also ties the citation to texts the committee can discuss. On Tawada, I agree that the unevenness of access across Japanese and German is a real obstacle, because wordplay and estrangement between languages are what translation carries least. I do not take this as a judgment on her inventiveness, only as a limit on how confidently we can credit her. That is why she is not among my two named alternatives.

responses.point: Carlberg warns that the density and length of Cărtărescu's prose may not carry in translation. She says a citation naming poetry would be partly unverified. She also cautions that Nobel's 'idealist' direction is open to broad interpretation and could favor almost any serious writer, and she wants the case to rest on voice, form and depth.
responses.response: I agree on all three points and have adjusted accordingly. The citation should credit what survives translation, namely the architecture, the imaginative logic and the sustained invention, and be modest about sentence-level music. I have dropped poetry from the citation text. I also do not use the 'idealist' direction as a separate argument. The case rests on voice, formal achievement and depth, and it would stand or fall on those. Her note that Adonis remains a durable case on literary grounds fits my own view, and it is part of why he is one of my two alternatives.

responses.point: Sward keeps Zurita as her first alternative. She says the citation must rest on the written sequences, Purgatory and Anteparadise, and that the landscape and sky-written works are known mostly through description and so should count as context.
responses.response: I agree and would say it plainly: if Zurita were the laureate, the citation would have to rest on the written poems, with the landscape works named as part of the practice and not as the ground of the award. I read her remark that Cărtărescu's texts are more fully available to us than Zurita's extra-textual work as a fair point about evidence. Where we may differ is on what follows if the repetition concern proves well founded. In that case I would move to Zurita before others, because a concentrated project of decades can be tested on the written sequences. I would not move on moral weight or historical context, which are not literary criteria.

uncertainties: I have not read the Romanian originals or independently verified any source. All judgments rest on public knowledge and translation, including my provisional view that Solenoid changes the mode of the earlier trilogy.
Whether the later long fictions develop or repeat the earlier project is unresolved. The record does not settle it, and no member has offered close readings of specific passages.
Poetry and early work are thinly covered in translation, which is why the citation now rests on prose.

For the alternatives, Zurita's landscape works are hard to weigh as literature, and Spanish and Arabic verse lose rhythm and prosody in translation. Adonis's late collections are only partly surveyed here.
The six members share the same translations and reservations. Agreement among us may reflect correlated judgment and is not independent evidence of merit.
Carlberg is a co-opted member whose committee voting status is undocumented. The six-vote structure and the four-vote majority are modeling assumptions.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile, which records no personal, institutional or professional tie to any shortlisted writer. I update the round-1 note with one disclosure for transparency. My own fiction is Central European and historical, and I have lived in Prague and Vienna, so the region of Cărtărescu's work is geographically close to my own background. I treat that as context and not as evidence of preference, and I do not claim any tie to him. My 2025 prize remarks about another writer's syntax reflect a collective official position or a different case. I do not apply that standard to this shortlist automatically. Conflicts are disclosed here, not adjudicated.
